summary: The bench never measures RLS: it runs as the compose superuser, and its policy breaks for a real app role
detail: compose.yml makes delta the bootstrap superuser, so every adapter in bench/run.ts (and the published results-0.3.0.md) ran with the policy bypassed. Run as a NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS role, the bench policy throws 22P02: after a transaction-local set_config commits, a pooled connection reads app.user_id as '' not NULL, and ''::int fails; rls.md prescribes NULLIF(current_setting('app.user_id', true), '')::int. Fix: (1) NULLIF in bench/schema.ts; (2) run the adapters as an app role (two pools as rls.md: admin for applyFramework, schema and seed; app role with USAGE/DML and EXECUTE for writeOp), by BENCH_APP_PG_URL or SET ROLE; (3) refuse to run when rolsuper or rolbypassrls; (4) correct bench/README.md and relabel or re-run results-0.3.0.md. Measured (PG 16, loopback): RLS adds ~5 us to a static UPDATE but ~490 us (~20%) to a delta_apply_as write, the generic engine re-planning the policy in its dynamic queries. Acceptance: bun run bench passes as a NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS role, refuses a superuser or BYPASSRLS role, and the README and results say what is measured. Note 2026-10-15: Postgres is moving to dzql (compiled); this bench, and the 20% it found, go with it.

summary: An undo or redo walked every chain its cursor ever began to find its entry: it slowed as the cursor's ledger grew
detail: nextUndo/nextRedo ran a recursive CTE over every chain the cursor began (1 ms at 3,000 entries of one cursor, 3.3 ms at 10,000). Ported dzql's fix (blueshed/dzql#35, _delta_ledger_tip): newest first among the cursor's own entries on its (cursor, id) index, skip an entry something walked, depth up undoes to the chain's write (this cursor's, undoable), back an even depth, forward an odd one undoable, a redo stops at the cursor's last write. Proved equal to the old query over seeded runs through the API; a long history's lookup takes ~30-40 SQLite VM steps where the old took ~120,000 (sqlite3_stmt_status via bun:ffi).

summary: A document cannot show a fact that comes from another parent's rows: whether a tool is out, from its open loans
detail: The shed's list of tools needs, for each tool, whether it is out and when it is due back. A loan hangs from its member, and a row has one parent, so the tools document cannot include the open loans. Every session stores the fact on the tool (tools.out, tools.due) and writes it in the same change as the loan: consistent through the app's own writes, a second copy all the same. Options: a document that includes rows reached by a key other than the parent (a 'referenced by' include), a derived field the backend computes, or the evolve skill teaching the same-change write as the pattern. Decide which; all three backends (JSON, SQLite, dzql) answer alike.
note: 2026-10-16: found by The Shed, a held-out example told as stories and built by fresh sessions from paintbrush to dzql (paintbrush evals/shed, runs/2026-10-16-opus-5.5.md).

summary: A data migration has to create the tables and columns it fills: migrations run before the schema adds what it declares
detail: The Shed's stage 4 migrations: 002 makes a strimmer a kit by inserting parts rows, so it first writes CREATE TABLE parts by hand ('as delta's createTables makes it'); 001 fills a due date, so it first writes ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN. The order (migrate first, then createTables / migrateSchema) is documented and right for renames and drops; a data migration into something the new schema declares needs the schema's additions first. Options: migrate(db, migrations, { schema }) adds what the schema declares before running the data steps, or a migration declares it needs the schema applied first.
note: 2026-10-16: found by The Shed, a held-out example told as stories and built by fresh sessions from paintbrush to dzql (paintbrush evals/shed, runs/2026-10-16-opus-5.5.md).

summary: The schema cannot declare a unique constraint: two sheds lending one tool at once are stopped by a hand-written index
detail: Stage 5 (two servers on one Postgres) needs 'a tool is on one open loan at a time'. The session wrote CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_loan_per_tool ON lent (tool) WHERE returned IS NULL by hand, beside dzql's generated SQL. A unique (and partial unique) declaration in defineSchema, honoured by SQLite and by dzql's generateSql, would say it once.

summary: Migrations the Django way: the history starts from empty, and the compiler writes each migration from the change in the definitions
detail: Today the schema is applied implicitly at every start (SQLite's migrateSchema, Postgres's generateSql with IF NOT EXISTS / ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS), and a migration is only what a schema cannot say. On a fresh database migrate records every migration as run and runs none. So the schema's history is split three ways and no one place says how a database got here. The Shed showed the cost: stage 5 moved to Postgres with no migrations at all, sign-in's tables and the one-loan index were hand-written at start, and a data migration had to create the tables it fills (#80). Peter's direction (2026-10-16): as Django does, migration 001 creates the tables from empty with IF NOT EXISTS (so a database that already has them adopts it as run, changing nothing); every later change is a numbered migration, which the compiler writes deterministically from the difference between the definitions and the last migration (makemigrations), edited by a person only for what a diff cannot know (a rename, a data fill); a fresh database runs them all from 001; nothing is applied implicitly at start. Settles #80 (a data migration follows the one that makes its table) and gives #81's unique constraint a home. Then paintbrush's Postgres step (paintbrush #12) teaches it, and the Shed's next run adds a stage that changes a running Postgres. Design as a plan for Peter to read before it is built; after dzql 2c.
